sections.heading: The idea
sections.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a column of two labels</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">p</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">q</text></svg>
sections.body_md:
Gauss-Newton minimizes a sum of squared residuals by refusing to solve the nonlinear problem directly. At the current point it replaces the residual vector by its linear model, the value plus the Jacobian times a step, and it chooses the step that makes that model as small as possible in the least-squares sense. The model is a linear least-squares problem, so the step comes from the normal equations. The point then moves by that step, the residual and the Jacobian are rebuilt, and the same linear fit is repeated.

The gradient of \(\tfrac12\lVert r\rVert^2\) is \(J_r^T r\). Whenever the Jacobian has full column rank and this gradient is not zero, the Gauss-Newton step is a descent direction. Its directional derivative equals the negative of a squared norm built from the gradient and the inverse of \(J_r^T J_r\). A short move along the step therefore decreases the sum of squares. Full column rank can fail. The Gram matrix is always positive semidefinite, but it may be singular, and then the normal equations do not determine one step.

Newton's method on the same sum of squares uses a richer Hessian. Besides \(J_r^T J_r\), the true Hessian adds each residual component times the second derivative of that component. Gauss-Newton keeps only the Gram matrix. The dropped term is zero when every component is affine, and it is also zero when the residual itself is zero. A curved residual that is still large makes the two steps differ.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
The step solves
\[
J_r^T J_r\, d = -J_r^T r.
\]
The true Hessian of \(\tfrac12\lVert r\rVert^2\) is \(J_r^T J_r + \sum_i r_i \nabla^2 r_i\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Take the residual \((u^2 - 7,\ u - 4)\) at \(u = 1\). The value is \((-6,\ -3)\) and the Jacobian column is \((2,\ 1)\). The Gram entry is \(4 + 1 = 5\), and the gradient entry is \(2\cdot(-6) + 1\cdot(-3) = -15\). The normal equation \(5d = 15\) gives the step \(3\).

The hatch step is 3. The updated parameter is \(4\). The residual there is \((9,\ 0)\), not zero, so the nonlinear fit is not finished. The linear model was exact only for the tangent, and the square in the first component has already curved away from that tangent.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: The normal equation carries a minus sign. Solving \(J^T J\, d = J^T r\) walks up the linear model. A second slip is to invert a singular Gram matrix. Positive semidefinite is not the same as invertible, and a zero column in the Jacobian is enough to make the matrix singular. A third is to expect one step to land on a root of a curved residual. The example moves to a point whose residual is still nonzero. A fourth is to treat \(J_r^T J_r\) as the full Hessian. The missing term is the one that involves second derivatives of the components.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: When the Gram matrix is nearly singular, the plain step becomes long and the linear model stops being a trustworthy picture of the residual. Adding a positive multiple of the identity shortens that step and bends it toward steepest descent. That damped step is Levenberg-Marquardt. A different use of the same exact step appears when each new block is already linear: one Gauss-Newton step finishes the block, and chaining those steps is recursive least squares.
